title: Binary Counter Exhibit
story: A science museum has a wall of light bulbs that counts in binary. Each second it shows the next number: 0, then 1, then 10, then 11, then 100, and so on, with a lit bulb for every 1 bit.
The museum's electrician is planning the power supply. For a show that counts from 0 up to n, she wants to know how many bulbs are lit at each number.
task: Write litBulbs(n). Return a list of length n + 1 where position i holds the number of 1 bits in the binary form of i.
Aim for O(n) total time: work out each count from a count you already have, instead of examining every bit of every number.

examples.explanation: The count drops back to 1 at 4 and at 8. Each power of two lights one bulb, after a run where many bulbs were lit (7 = 111 has three).

hints: Write 6 and 3 in binary: 110 and 11. Then 10 and 5: 1010 and 101. How is each pair related, and what does that do to the number of 1 bits?
i >> 1 (that is, i divided by 2, rounded down) is i with its last bit chopped off. Every other bit stays the same.
So the bulbs lit for i are the bulbs lit for i >> 1, plus one more if the bit you chopped off was a 1. How do you read that last bit?
Fill the list from 0 upward: counts[0] = 0, and counts[i] = counts[i >> 1] + (i & 1). i >> 1 is always smaller than i, so its count is already there.
bruteForce: For each number from 0 to n, count its 1 bits one at a time: check the last bit, shift right, repeat until the number is 0.

Each number takes up to about 17 steps when n is 100,000, so this is O(n log n). It is not slow, but it throws away work: the count for 12 already contains the count for 6, which you computed a moment ago.

tests.note: ends on a power of two

walkthrough: Shifting right by one drops the last bit and keeps the rest. So every number shares all but one bit with a smaller number whose count you already know.
A tempting shortcut is "one more bulb than the previous number". It fails at every carry: 7 has three bulbs lit, but 8 has only one.
solution.timeWhy: One shift, one AND and one addition per number.
solution.spaceWhy: Nothing beyond the output list itself.
solution.takeaway: When answers for smaller inputs are hiding inside bigger ones, build a table from small to large and reuse it. Here the link is a single shift: the bits of i are the bits of i >> 1 plus one more.
